slides.title: - Suppose I have a problem with 4 binary features and 2 classes
slides.content: - Suppose I have a problem with 4 binary features and 2 classes - Possible examples = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16 - Possible ways to label= 2 x 2 x … x 2 = 216 = 65536 - Observing part of the data does not rule out much - E.g. We observe 7 labeled examples, this leaves 9 unobserved examples →29 possible labelings still left - How can we decide which model is best? Faculteit, departement, dienst … 43 Fundamental challenge of learning

slides.title: - We need to make assumptions: experience alone doesn’t allow us to make
slides.content: - We need to make assumptions: experience alone doesn’t allow us to make conclusions about unseen data instances - Two types of bias - Restriction: Limit the hypothesis space (Rules, straight lines, parabolas, …) - Preference: Impose an ordering on the hypothesis space (e.g. Simpler models) Faculteit, departement, dienst … 44 Solution: Inductive Bias

slides.title: - At high-level, algorithms learn one of these:
slides.content: - At high-level, algorithms learn one of these: - Function that predicts class or real value (e.g. decision tree, linear regression) - Conditional probability distribution P(Y|X) (e.g. logistic regression, neural network) - Joint probability distribution P(X,Y) (e.g. Naïve Bayes) Faculteit, departement, dienst … 45 Goals of learning

slides.title: - At high-level, algorithms learn one of these:

slides.title: - Typically we have two high-level components:
slides.content: - Typically we have two high-level components: - How well does the model fit the data? - How “complex” is the model? - Tradeoff fit (good) for complexity (bad) - In an ideal case: perfect fit without complexity - E.g. rule learning: #positives covered - #negatives covered - #literals - 𝑥1 ∨𝑥2 ∨𝑥3 ⟹𝑌 #P = 20 #N = 10 - 𝑥1 ∨𝑥3 ∧𝑥2 ∨𝑥4 ∧𝑥1 ∨𝑥2 ⟹𝑌 #P = 21 #N = 9 Faculteit, departement, dienst … 50 Evaluating candidate models

slides.title: - A loss function quantifies the impact or consequence of an error (incorrect prediction)
slides.content: - A loss function quantifies the impact or consequence of an error (incorrect prediction) - E.g. 0/1-loss is 0 if correct, 1 if incorrect. The average 0/1-loss over a dataset is the classification error rate. - Goal is to find - a hypothesis h in hypothesis space ℋ - that minimizes some loss ℓ on the data - with r(h) the model size and 𝜆 the weight of this model size Faculteit, departement, dienst … 51 Evaluation of a model often framed in terms of loss

slides.title: - Weird things happen in high dimensions because our intuitions from low-
slides.content: - Weird things happen in high dimensions because our intuitions from low- dimensions do not translate - Generally, adding dimensions (features) creates many problems for learners - One big problem: with lots of features, one can end up with spurious correlations - kNNs are easily misled with high-dimensional spaces - Density lowers → distances flatten and all examples become equidistant - Not the case when the distribution of positives has low variance Faculteit, departement, dienst … 115 Problem 3: Curse of dimensionality

slides.title: - kNN is very slow
slides.content: - kNN is very slow - Complexity is O(nd) with n the number of examples and d the dimension - All training examples should be in memory - Solutions (see course on Big Data Analytics Programming for more details) - Efficient retrieval structures (KD trees, …) - Locality sensitive hashing (use hashing to identify neighbors) - Product quantization (Compress data, approximate distance based on embedding) Faculteit, departement, dienst … 116 Problem 4

slides.title: - Advantages
slides.content: - Advantages - Training is fast - Learns complex target functions easily - Can predict discrete, real values, probabilities (dependent on distance measure) - Online or incremental learning is possible - Shares elements of human reasoning - Disadvantages - Test time is very slow - Large memory cost - No explicit model to inspect Faculteit, departement, dienst … 117 Pros and Cons of kNN

slides.title: Data: (X,Y) examples
slides.content: Data: (X,Y) examples → Representation: choose features → Inductive bias: nearby examples have similar outputs → Model/learner: lazy, instance-based → Choices: k, distance measure, feature scaling/weighting → Prediction: find k nearest examples + combine labels → Evaluation: validation/test performance → Pitfalls: scaling, irrelevant features, dimensionality, computational cost Faculteit, departement, dienst … 118 Supervised learning with kNN
